demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: Mark is a 34-year-old school counselor who has been struggling with profound psychological distress following an incident where he accidentally caused serious injury to another individual. This traumatic event continues to haunt him, and his symptoms have become increasingly debilitating over time. The accident occurred at a local community sports event when Mark was coaching a youth baseball team. In the heat of the moment, he made a decision that led to one of the players being severely injured. The intense stress and shock from this incident has left deep psychological scars. Since then, any form of medical procedures or related smells trigger vivid memories of the accident. These triggers are particularly potent because they bring back the overwhelming fear and guilt associated with the event. Mark's coping mechanisms have become maladaptive over time as he tries to manage these triggers. He constantly keeps his mind occupied with work-related tasks and other activities, which serves both as a distraction from intrusive thoughts and memories and as a way to avoid thinking about what happened. This mental preoccupation helps him navigate through the day but has started to take a toll on his relationships and job performance. For instance, during a recent medical check-up at the hospital, the sterile smell of antiseptic immediately transported Mark back to the emergency room where he had seen the injured player. He experienced intense physical reactions—sweating, rapid heartbeat, and nausea—and struggled to stay focused. The memory felt so real that it was as if the event were happening again in the present moment. The intensity of these memories has left him with a sense of self-doubt. Mark is certain that he cannot trust himself to make the right decisions anymore. This belief compounds his fear and anxiety, making it even more difficult for him to cope with daily life. He feels as though his life has been irrevocably destroyed by this trauma, and these negative appraisals exacerbate his feelings of guilt and self-blame. His negative appraisals have influenced his maladaptive strategies. The constant need for mental distraction arises from a deep-seated belief that he cannot handle the memories and emotions tied to the accident. By keeping himself busy with work or other activities, Mark hopes to avoid the intense emotional pain and fear associated with the event. This cycle of thoughts and behaviors has created a self-reinforcing loop where his triggers lead to vivid, full-sensory reliving of the memory. These memories then fuel his negative appraisals and physical reactions, which in turn increase his reliance on maladaptive strategies like mental distraction. The result is an overwhelming sense of vigilance and fear, especially at night when he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels a need to stay alert. As Mark’s symptoms have intensified over time, the impact on his daily life has become more pronounced. His wife reports that he has been distant and irritable, and this strain in their relationship is evident. At work, Mark finds it increasingly challenging to focus on counseling students effectively due to his constant mental preoccupation with thoughts of the accident. What finally brought Mark to seek help was a recent episode where he experienced a severe panic attack during a school event. He realized that if he did not address these issues, they would continue to erode his quality of life and relationships further. He is most afraid of never being able to trust himself again or fully escape the memories and guilt associated with the accident. Mark hopes for relief from the constant distress and a way to rebuild his confidence and ability to function effectively in his role as a school counselor and in his personal life. He recognizes that professional help might be the key to breaking this cycle of avoidance, negative appraisals, and intense emotional reactivity.
